title: Language Strategy in Multinational Company
sourceHeading: Language Strategy in a Multinational Company

source.filename: Practice 141 - IETLS 閱讀練習 - Passage 2.pdf

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The importance of language management in multinational companies has never been greater. Multinationals are increasingly conscious of global coordination as a source of competitive advantage, yet language remains the ultimate barrier to international harmonisation. Before considering language-management strategies, companies must evaluate the magnitude of the language barrier confronting them. They need to examine three dimensions: language diversity, language penetration and language sophistication. Companies must then decide how best to manage language, choosing from a range of options when formulating their strategy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Lingua Franca: The simplest answer—though realistic only for English-speaking companies—is to rely on one’s native tongue. As recently as 1991, a survey of British exporting companies found that more than one-third used English exclusively in dealings with foreign customers. The attitude that ‘one language fits all’ has continued into the Internet age. A survey of the websites of leading American companies confirmed that more than half made no provision for access in foreign languages; another found that fewer than 10 per cent could respond adequately to emails written in a language other than the company’s. Although widespread, reliance on a single language is a fatally flawed strategy. It makes no allowance for growing linguistic nationalism, through which buyers—particularly in Asia, South America and the Middle East—assert their right to ‘work in the language of the customer’. It also ignores the increasing vitality of Spanish, Arabic and Chinese, which may eventually challenge English’s dominance as a lingua franca. In information technology, it disregards the Internet’s rapid globalisation: English-language e-commerce transactions, emails and websites are declining as a proportion of the total. Finally, total reliance on one language puts English speakers at risk during negotiations. Contracts, rules and legislation are invariably written in the local language, leaving any company unable to operate in that language vulnerable.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Functional Multilingualism: Another improvised approach is what has been called ‘functional multilingualism’. Essentially, this means muddling through by relying on a mixture of languages, pidgins and gestures—whatever means the parties have at their disposal. In a social setting, the shared effort to understand one another may aid bonding, with the frustrations of communication regularly punctuated by moments of absurdity and humour. As a basis for business negotiations, however, it is decidedly hit-and-miss. Nevertheless, Hagen’s recent study suggests that 16 per cent of international business transactions are conducted using a ‘cocktail of languages’. Functional multilingualism shares the defects of relying on a lingua franca and increases the probability of cognitive divergence between the parties.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: External Language Resources: A more rational and obvious response to the language barrier is to employ external translators and interpreters; many excellent companies specialise in these fields. Such a response, however, does not eliminate the barrier. First, these services can be very expensive, with a leading simultaneous interpreter commanding daily rates as high as those of a partner in an international consulting firm. Second, a good translator or interpreter will insist that, to be fully effective, they must understand the context of the subject matter. This is not always possible. The complexity or specialisation of the topic may prevent it; sometimes there is too little preparation time, but most often the obstacle is the parties’ reluctance to explain the wider context to an outsider. Unless the interpreter and the clients have been extensively briefed, ambiguity and cultural overtones may remain in the source messages. The interpreter will, of course, endeavour to provide a high-fidelity translation, but in such circumstances must use initiative and guesswork, introducing a potential source of misunderstanding. Finally, although a good interpreter will try to convey both the meaning and spirit of a communication, rhetorical power is inevitably lost when it passes through a third party. In situations requiring negotiation, persuasion or humour, an interpreter is therefore a poor substitute for direct communication.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Training: An understandable first response to a skills shortage is personnel development, and the language-training industry is well established, offering programmes at almost every level and in numerous languages. Without doubting the value of such training, however, no company should assume that it guarantees success. Training in most companies follows the economic cycle: when times are good, money is invested; when belts tighten, training is one of the first ‘luxuries’ to be cut. In a study conducted across four European countries, nearly twice as many companies said they would need language training in the coming years as had provided it in previous years. This disparity between ‘good intentions’ and ‘actual delivery’ underlines the problems of relying on training for language skills. Unless a company is fully committed to sustaining the strategy through difficult times, it will fail.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: One notable and committed leader in language training is the Volkswagen Group. It has developed a language strategy over many years and, in many respects, provides a model of professional language management. The Volkswagen approach emphasises that language training must be considered a strategic rather than a tactical solution. Its system requires completion of six language stages to progress from ‘basics’ to ‘communication competence’. Each stage demands approximately 90 hours of refresher instruction, supported by many more hours of self-study over six to nine months. Completion of every stage is marked by an achievement test, a prerequisite for further training. Even this professionally managed programme expects a minimum of three years of fairly intensive study to produce an accountant, engineer, buyer or salesperson capable of working effectively in a foreign language. Companies pursuing this route therefore need realistic expectations and an intention to sustain the programme for many years. Except for ‘brush-up’ courses for people who were previously fluent, training is not a quick fix, so other methods must also be considered.
